title: Kishkindha Kanda: The Alliance of the Vanaras
body:
Kishkindha Kanda: The Alliance of the Vanaras

29. Sugriva-mitra-pujita Rama
31. Hanumad-pujita-charana Rama
32. Vali-prana-harana-karana Rama
33. Sugriva-sharanagata-pala-ka Rama
34. Tara-grief-shamana-karana Rama

The Slaying of Vali and the Dundubhi Test

Rama and Lakshmana reached the Rishyamukha mountain, where they met Hanuman, the foremost monkey hero and a devotee of the exiled Sugriva. Hanuman immediately recognized the divine nature of the brothers and arranged a meeting with Sugriva. The two made a sacred pact of friendship over fire: Rama promised to help Sugriva regain his kingdom and his wife from his tyrannical brother Vali, while Sugriva pledged his vast army of Vanaras to search for Sita.
To prove his strength to Sugriva, who was deeply terrified of Vali's unmatched power, Rama performed two extraordinary feats. First, with a single kick, he sent the massive, dry skeleton of the demon Dundubhi flying over ten leagues. When Sugriva remained hesitant, noting that Vali had slain Dundubhi when the demon was in a fresh, powerful state, Rama smiled. He drew his bow and shot a single arrow through seven massive sal trees, piercing the earth and returning to his quiver. Astonished and filled with deep faith, Sugriva fell at his feet, ready to challenge his brother.
Sugriva challenged Vali to a duel. As the brothers fought fiercely, looking completely identical, Rama could not shoot. Hanuman placed a garland of wild flowers around Sugriva's neck, allowing Rama to distinguish them. From his hidden position behind a tree, Rama released his arrow, piercing Vali's chest.
The slaying of Vali from hiding remains one of the most debated ethical questions of the epic. As Vali lay dying, he questioned Rama's dharma: 'You are a prince of the Ikshvaku line, renowned for your justice. Why did you strike me from a hidden position, like a hunter preying on an animal?' Rama gently knelt beside him, explaining that Vali had violated the laws of righteousness by taking his own brother's wife while his brother was still alive—an act that reduced him to the level of an animal. To punish such a transgression of the moral order, the standard rules of warrior combat did not apply. Understanding the deeper truth of Rama's words, Vali begged for forgiveness, entrusted his son Angada to Rama's care, and passed away in peace.

Tara's Wisdom and the Monsoon of Grief

Following Vali's death, Sugriva was crowned king. However, swept up in the intoxication of power and luxury, he forgot his promise to Rama as the monsoon rains came and went. Rama waited in the cold cave, his heart filled with grief for Sita.
It was Tara, Vali's wise widow and the new queen, who stepped forward to save the kingdom. While Sugriva cowered in fear, Tara calmly faced the raging Lakshmana, speaking words of profound diplomacy: 'Do not yield to anger, O noble prince. Sugriva is indeed at fault, but his love for Rama is true. We are ready to fulfill our pledge.' Her eloquence and calm grace completely disarmed Lakshmana's wrath. Sugriva immediately apologized, and vast search parties were dispatched to the four corners of the earth. The southern party, led by the crown prince Angada, Hanuman, and the wise Jambavan, learned from the vulture Sampati—Jatayu's elder brother—that Sita was held across the sea in the island kingdom of Lanka.
